extracted.intended_audience: computer-science/math researchers and students who write technical papers and books
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for composing, revising, and publishing technical papers and books in computer science and related fields, covering style, structure, ethics (plagiarism), audience choice, and pedagogical exercises to improve writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the market and know thyself
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of prevailing practices in similar texts but do not slavishly imitate another’s style; work out a compromise between market expectations and your own voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: “Don’t slavishly imitate another’s style, but don’t avoid it either. Know the market, know thyself, and work out a compromise of your own. Don’t hesitate to follow the crowd when they are all going in the right direction.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism — avoid verbatim borrowing and suspicious coincidences
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation becomes culpable plagiarism if a reasonable person would believe you had the original work open while writing; you cannot copyright ideas, only expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: quoting verbatim without attribution, reproducing a dozen successive equations from another source, or using identical typography/italics/notation can be damning. For survey papers, verbatim quotes are acceptable if the writer is not presenting the work as their own, and be explicit in quotations if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting/typographic identity can imply copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-substantive matches between works (e.g., identical use of italics, coincident notation) can be evidence of improper borrowing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to incidental stylistic matches; correcting a typo in an otherwise identical sentence may be insufficient to dispel suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second editions — reuse with care and expect work
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent editions consume effort but can reuse earlier examples; they also restart the commercial life of a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jeff: “these will still consume a kilohour or so, although they’ll go faster if you can use your earlier examples.” Financially advantageous because people stop buying older books after a few years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not write papers for bad motivations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing just to increase publication count or to get a paper into a particular conference; these motives often produce sloppy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie's two bad reasons: (1) “to have a long publications list,” and (2) “to have a paper published in a specific conference.” Both can lead to poor quality and sloppiness; integrity/self-policing is urged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish because you are excited about the work
rubrics_metrics.description: A good reason to publish is that you have done something you are genuinely excited about and want to share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie: “You have done something that you are excited about.” Also: judge on what you decide not to publish as a sign of discernment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn to write by reading widely (study good literature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop writing skill more like learning piano than typing: spend time reading excellent writing (including literature) to sharpen style and craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie cites Halmos, Knuth, Fowles, Eliot as valuable reading. Reading great literature helps learn how to write good mathematical literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad writing comes from bad thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity of thought precedes clear writing; you must know what you want to present before you can present it well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ideas are unclear, fixing prose alone won’t help. Keep in mind the content and the audience when writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate publication venue
rubrics_metrics.description: Select venue based on readiness and purpose: journals for polished, timeless work; conferences for rougher, preliminary results; technical reports for work not ready for the general world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie: “Journal articles should be polished and timeless. Conference papers can be a little rougher… Technical reports are good for work that is not even ready for the general world but still should be written up.” Always remember that there are readers in each case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conceits/themes sparingly and be willing to abandon them
rubrics_metrics.description: A conceit (a fanciful idea around which a paper is built) can catalyze writing but should not intrude; avoid cute conceits and jokes that may age poorly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of jokes—how funny will a joke be ten years later? Use conceits to present ideas, not to distract from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include concrete examples — better one solid example than abstract dryness
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples keep you honest and clarify ideas; it is better to have a solid, simple example than only abstract exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie: “It is better to have one solid example than to have a dry, abstract, academic paper.” Use simple examples (80-20 rule) and ensure your theory handles the example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the idea before fixing the sentence; prioritize structure over formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on clarifying ideas and overall structure rather than obsessing about formatting during drafting; use macros for complex notation to avoid low-level distractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie: “Don’t think about format. Do think about structure.” Use macros for complex notation and let structural clarity guide formatting later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use notation and presentation tools to make structure clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebra and notation are tools to present structure succinctly; consider structural forms (e.g., tabular proofs) that enforce clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamport showed paragraph vs tabular (statement-reason) proofs; tabular proofs are easier to read and can help clarify paragraph proofs. Consider the overall discourse structure, not just formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a strong, nontechnical, direct first sentence; avoid passive voice
rubrics_metrics.description: The first sentence should show excitement, be simple and direct, and avoid passive weakness; sustain that quality throughout the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie: first sentences should “leap out” and be nontechnical. “Avoid passive wimpiness.” Once you hook a reader, subsequent sentences must maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not spend more than a year on any project
rubrics_metrics.description: A time-management maxim: avoid protracted projects; don’t spend more than one year on any single thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributed as Jeff's maxim: “Never spend more than a year on anything.” Use this as a guardrail against overlong efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start early
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin writing early and cultivate the habit; early starts allow the writing compulsion to organize material and improve work over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nils: “Start early. Impressionable minds are best. Some people find that writing becomes a compulsion; if this happens to you, then let the urge take over!”

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrite repeatedly and seek critique before publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect to rewrite many times; rarely is first draft final. Always get others to critique your work before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nils: “Write, rewrite, rewrite… Never let anything you write be published without having had others critique it.” Use departmental colleagues or external reviewers to catch oversights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach the material or present it while writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching a topic while writing it helps clarify and organize the material; course preparation is a productive companion to writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nils: try to teach a course on the topic while writing; lecturing and talking through the material reveals weaknesses and shapes exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read extensively to sharpen style and critical faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading widely improves writing skill, style, and the ability to critique your own work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nils: reading great literature and technical writing develops taste and craft; “Read a great deal; it’ll sharpen your style.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Model the reader — anticipate misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: Constantly ask how a reader will misunderstand your text; run background mental checks to catch likely confusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nils’s “daemons”: mental checks that automatically flag problems (e.g., split infinitives, confusing notation). Develop these by practice so checking becomes automatic, not compulsive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the medium — vocabulary, graphs, typography, and indices
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn tools beyond words: the right vocabulary, effective graphs, typographic conventions and indices to aid readers’ comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need a good vocabulary (not necessarily many big words). Use typography (e.g., typewriter font) to distinguish logical formulae and graphs/indices to communicate structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Master the material — writing clarifies understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing is part of thinking; organizing material for publication deepens your internal model and understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities like giving talks, taking courses, and re-organizing text provide internal feedback. Quotation: “How do I know what I mean until I hear what I say?”

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify initial exposition, then elaborate
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with a straightforward, possibly simplified presentation to get readers on board, and add details later to repay simplifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple examples to convey the bulk of the idea (80-20 rule). Nils: “Lie, if it helps… present the reader with something straightforward to start off with.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid recycling old material without rewriting for new context
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist reusing chunks of old text verbatim; new context demands rewrite and adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if online editors make reuse easy, the emphasis and context often differ — rewrite to reflect new perspective and improved skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for excellence and continual improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain high standards; strive for better even if perfection is unattainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotations from Hemingway, McPhee, etc.: keep shooting for perfection; be never fully satisfied and continually push quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary and syntax mastery through exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase command of vocabulary and especially syntactic variety via deliberate exercises (vocabulary substitution, thesaurus entry, syntactic recasting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire: focus on syntactic ‘armory’ not only vocabulary breadth; perform exercises such as swapping words in a composition and writing thesaurus entries over a week.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-length targets and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for sentence-length averages under ~20 words (ideal 15–18) and strong variation across sentences to achieve good pacing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire: study 10 sentences on page 3 of papers; aim for 9–10 different lengths among 10 sentences; variation between shortest and longest might range broadly but ideal distribution is bell-shaped around 15–18 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid syntactic monotony; vary sentence templates and constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the same sentence construction repeatedly; seek diverse sentence templates and judicious use of parallels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two authors with similar averages can differ: one may use identical constructions repeatedly (bad), while another varies constructions (better). Use tight parallels intentionally but don’t overuse unusual constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentences and high-literary forms are usually inappropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic sentence forms (where grammatical and physical ends coincide) are a high literary mode and generally unsuitable for technical writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are more common in church or literary prose; be aware of their effect and use sparingly if at all in technical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control emphasis by recasting sentences — front and back are emphatic positions
rubrics_metrics.description: To change emphasis in a sentence, recast it; the front and end positions carry emphasis while the middle is less emphatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire’s exercises include recasting to shift emphasis; practice to discover the effective positions for your key points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual-labor techniques: copying, memorizing, and recitation to deepen reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Use manual exercises (typing or longhand copying, memorization, recitation) to slow down and analyze text closely and to internalize style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typing or writing passages forces careful reading. Auden: copying a poem on a typewriter shows contempt; copying longhand shows admiration. These techniques aid deep comprehension and style absorption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aloud and peer-listening partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Read writing aloud to partners and listen to each other; limited, focused feedback sessions can yield strong benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some will be embarrassed, others will gain insight; form partnerships and limit the exposure to what is productive for both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scansion, verse, and précis exercises to improve economy and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice scansion and even verse to develop rhythm and concision; use précis exercises to reduce word counts while preserving essential meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leslie touched on précis: reducing word count inevitably changes structure at various reduction percentages—practice to learn the structural thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nearly-real exercises (e.g., joke writing) for pure exposition practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform near-real tasks like composing jokes, which are strict exposition exercises, to hone expository clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire: “Writing a joke is exposition at its purest. Things aren’t funny unless they are well written.” These exercises simulate stakes of real writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ben Franklin-style memory reconstruction exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewrite a passage from memory with limited hints to test comprehension and to compare your version with the original for improvement points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mary-Claire suggests trying this with known authors’ passages (e.g., Don’s writing) to see what you prefer in each version and to diagnose stylistic strengths and weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce grammar correctness under pressure (example: which vs that)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice distinguishing commonly misused constructions (e.g., ‘which’ vs ‘that’) because under pressure usage degrades and signals nervousness or carelessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’s quiz: students wrote sentences to demonstrate correct use of ‘that’ and ‘which’; Mary-Claire notes people tend to use spoken forms correctly but revert under stress on paper.
